newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Kuchma expects to name new premier by mid-July.
newsitem.headline: Kuchma expects to name new premier by mid-July.

text.p: Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma, who accepted his reform-shy prime minister's resignation last week, said on Thursday he believed he could nominate a replacement within days.

Kuchma also told a news conference at the second Central and Eastern European Economic Summit he was confident Ukraine would reach agreement with the International Monetary Fund over a delayed $2.5-3 billion loan.
He said it should be possible to name a successor to former premier Pavlo Lazarenko after discussions on Friday with parliamentary factions.

"I will do my best to name this candidate before the parliamentary vacation (in the middle of July) and I think this will be possible after tomorrow's talks with leaders of the factions," Kuchma said, speaking through an interpreter.

Kuchma accepted Lazarenko's resignation on July 2 on health grounds and said a new phase of economic reform would begin. The president had been under increasing Western and domestic pressure to remove Lazarenko, said to be partly to blame for a slow pace in economic reforms, particularly in privatisation.
Ukraine, a former Soviet republic, is hoping to secure a $2.5-3 billion Extended Fund Facility loan from the IMF but it has been delayed as parliament only approved this year's budget on June 27.
The Fund has said it may issue a second, smaller stand-by loan unless it meets a number of conditions by next week. But Kuchma reiterated his confidence the loan would be made.
"I have got no doubt this programme will go on working," Kuchma said, adding he hoped the IMF would base future decisions on economic realities.

"There are problems in every country and there will be a defeat if we do not take them into account. I do not think it would be nice for the IMF if it was defeated on its programme for Ukraine," he added.

Asked if a new prime minister could herald a change in economic policy, Kuchma, who celebrated three years in power on Thursday, said he had said in June that Ukraine would maintain the path it had set out in October 1994.
"So far I have no doubt that this is the only possible track for Ukraine," he said.
Kuchma hailed the signing on Wednesday of a charter between Ukraine and the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO).
"This is a good sign that Ukraine is not alone, that Ukraine is one of the European family," he said.
He said the charter could also bring Ukraine economic benefits.
"I believe it to be a sort of protection for foreign investment from the NATO members states as well."
